    I spend a lot of time talking with builders who tell me they don’t really do marketing. Usually they say it with pride: “We’ve never had to. All of our work comes from word of mouth.”.

    My first response is usually that this is a good thing. If you’ve spent years building a organization where past clients, architects, and trade partners keep sending work your way, you’ve built something valuable. In construction, reputation matters, and that kind of trust is earned over time. I would never tell a builder to replace that with advertising.

    In a recent development, but I have also seen construction companies reach a point where the business landscape has changed, and reputation alone is not leading to the right clients. Good builders often struggle because the right people don’t know they exist.

    The phone may still be ringing, but the work coming in doesn’t always match where the organization wants to go next. The business has evolved, but what people know about it hasn’t necessarily evolved with it.

    Those are the moments when someone usually states, often a little reluctantly, “I guess we need to do some marketing.” That may indeed be the case. But I think there is a simpler and more useful way to frame the problem: Are you known for the work you actually want to do? That is where I would start.

    I’ve spent more than 20 years helping businesses and organizations grow, evolve, and connect with the people they want to reach, from owning and running a design and marketing agency to leading a destination marketing organization and working across marketing, branding, organizational leadership, consulting, and coaching. Today, as director of marketing and a business consultant with HELM Construction Solutions, I bring those experiences together in my work with builders, helping them think about where their business is going, the work they want more of, and what makes them different.

    In a recent development, sit across the table with an experienced builder and you swiftly understand what makes them different. But if you haven’t had that conversation, how would you know? I see this all the time: Some of the most valuable things about a construction tech giant live almost entirely in the owner’s head. The challenge is making more of that knowledge visible.

    Recent findings suggest that before I talk with a builder about websites, social media, advertising, or anything else that might get labeled “marketing,” I want to understand the business they are trying to build. What kind of work would they happily do again? Which projects are profitable? Which projects make the crew proud? Which clients trust the process? Where do they want to work? Who do they want to work alongside? What do they want the firm to look like in five years? And—just as crucial—what do they want less of?

    That last question can be surprisingly provocative. Construction companies are often encouraged to think about growth only in terms of more: more projects, more employees, more revenue, more leads. But growth doesn’t always mean more projects. Sometimes it means being more intentional about the work you take on.

    It has been revealed that I’ll ask why a builder does something a certain way, and suddenly we’re deep into a story about a detail, a process, or a hard-earned lesson that changed how they work. Those stories are usually where the good stuff is, and where what makes a manufacturer different becomes clear.

    It has been revealed that at this point, a lot of decisions get easier. You don’t need to reach everybody. You just need to become more visible to the people who value that kind of work.

    Industry observers note that if you aren’t sure how to identify the right types of projects for your business, I often suggest looking backward before looking forward. Choose three to five projects from the last few years that you would happily do again. Think about the jobs where the fit was right—the client trusted you, the work suited the strengths of your crew, the project was financially healthy, and the architect or designer was collaborative. Problems came up, as they always do, but the team solved them together rather than turning on one another. When the project ended, you were proud not only of what you built but of how you built it.

    Then ask a simple question: How did that project find us? You may discover that the same architect appears several times. Maybe a handful of past clients have been quietly sending people your way for years. Perhaps one designer, Realtor, supplier, or fellow builder keeps connecting you to projects that are an unusually good fit. Those patterns matter. They show you where to focus your time and attention. And when you’re trying to become known somewhere fresh, that kind of focus becomes even more notable.

    Industry observers note that for example, Sycamore Builders in western North Carolina has strong experience with architect-led custom homes in mountain communities. But as the company looks to expand into nearby markets, it faces a familiar challenge: Reputation is local.

    It has been revealed that in some of those communities, builders have been around for generations. Their trucks are familiar. Realtors and architects know them. Their projects are part of the landscape. That familiarity has been built over years. You cannot advertise your way into a 25-year relationship.

    Recent findings suggest that so Sycamore is taking a patient approach by building relationships with architects and Realtors, sharing more of the stories behind its work, and showing up consistently in a few specific communities. The goal isn’t a flood of calls. One or two well-aligned fresh builds a year can make a ­meaningful difference.

    According to recent reports, if the word marketing makes you want to stop reading, forget about marketing for a minute. Take an hour with your business partner, project manager, or someone who knows your manufacturer well and work through these questions. Let your answers guide you in pinpointing the type of work you want to find. Once you do, you won’t need to network every week, post every day, or constantly patch your website. Pick a few actions that fit your business, and keep doing them.

    What work do people call you for—and what work do you wish people called you for?

    Be honest with yourself. Is the work you’re doing now the work you want to be doing? If not, that’s your starting point.

    What are five projects you’d do again tomorrow?

    What made those projects good for the client, the crew, and the business? Writing the answers down can help you determine the type of work you want to do more of.

    How did each of those projects find you?

    It has been revealed that maybe it was a past client, an architect, a builder, a Realtor, a jobsite sign, a Google search, or something else. Don’t guess—find out. Then you can use those same methods to find similar projects in the future.

    Who is connected to the work you want?

    In a recent development, make a list of the Realtors, architects, designers, and trade partners who are connected to the kinds of projects and clients you want more of, using your favorite projects as a guide. Who do you already know? Who consistently connects you to good-fit work? Who would you like to build a stronger relationship with?

    How can you stay connected to those people?

    Recent findings suggest that could you invite someone to a jobsite, meet for coffee, share an interesting project over email, attend an industry event, or simply check in occasionally? Staying in touch helps potential partners remember you and your business when the right project comes along.

    When someone looks you up, can they see what you want to be known for?

    In a recent development, do your website and social media show the types of projects you want to do? Are you telling the stories behind that work and making your expertise visible? The clearer you are about the work you want, the easier it is for the right clients and partners to recognize that you’re the right fit.

    In a recent development, this is usually the point where someone says, “Carrie, I have houses to build. I can’t spend all my time updating a website, posting on social media, meeting architects for coffee, and telling project stories.”.

    Recent findings suggest that that’s fair, and I don’t want you to. Go back to what you learned about your best projects, and choose two or three things you can realistically keep doing to continue getting this sort of work. For example, maybe that means staying connected to a small group of architects and adding a strong project story to your website every few months.

    Industry observers note that then pay attention to what happens. Ask every new caller how they heard about you, notice which relationships lead to good-fit projects, and see whether the work coming through the door starts to look more like the work you want.

    For example, longtime high-performance builder Steve DeMetrick of DeMetrick Housewrights has spent more than two decades developing a reputation for building homes that demonstrate thoughtful craftsmanship, durability, and energy-efficiency. Most of his work has come through referrals. He has deep expertise, strong relationships, and plenty of experience. He is not trying to make the phone ring more.

    In fact, when we started talking about where he wants the manufacturer to go next, his answer was almost the opposite of what we typically associate with growth. He wants to slow down. He wants fewer projects at a time, larger scope, deeper involvement with each client, earlier collaboration with architects, and more opportunity to use the knowledge he has accumulated over decades.

    The more we talked, the clearer it became that high-performance construction is only part of what makes his company valuable. What really stands out is how he approaches the whole process—bringing design, budget, and scope together early and getting everyone working together sooner. That can lead to better decisions, fewer surprises, and a better experience for everyone involved. But that type of value is a lot harder to advertise on the side of a truck.

    The goal isn’t simply to tell more people that DeMetrick Housewrights builds high-performance homes. It is to make more of Steve’s thinking visible, to tell the stories behind projects, to explain why he approaches preconstruction the way he does, and to give potential clients and collaborators a better sense of what it is actually like to work with him. The point isn’t to create content for the sake of content. It is to help people see expertise that is already there.

    I’ve seen the same thing with Bell Street Builders in Maine, an employee-owned cooperative that does thoughtful restoration and renovation work around Portland and Casco Bay, including historic homes, architect-driven projects, and coastal and island construction. Those projects come with the kinds of challenges experienced builders know well: older structures that reveal surprises, coastal exposure, difficult logistics, complicated sequencing, and the need to make decisions carefully when clients may be living elsewhere.

    According to recent reports, when I worked on Bell Street’s strategic direction, one theme kept reappearing: Bell Street knows old buildings. This is much more useful than generically saying the company does “quality construction.”.

    Sources indicate that if you own a 100-year-old house in Portland and are about to open walls that may be hiding decades of issues, you want a builder who understands what they’re looking at and can respond without turning every surprise into a crisis. If you’re an architect working on that house, you want a builder who can solve problems collaboratively and respect the building while still moving the project forward.

    Bell Street did not need to become known to every homeowner in southern Maine. The better opportunity was to become more recognizable for the work the tech giant does best and in the places where it wants to do more of it. That meant making sure its website and social channels revealed more of its historic work and the stories behind complex projects, staying connected with architects and designers who work on those kinds of homes, and building relationships in priority communities such as Portland’s West End, Foreside communities, and the Casco Bay islands.

    Sources indicate that becoming recognizable doesn’t have to mean constantly creating something new. One good project can go a long way. Document the challenges during construction, photograph the finished work, explain what the team had to solve, and share that story on a website, social media, or directly with architects and past clients who may know someone planning a similar project.

    In a recent development, I genuinely appreciate builders’ resistance to marketing. It usually stems from a belief that the work should matter most. I think so too.

    A clever website cannot make up for poor craftsmanship. Advertising cannot replace trust, and social media cannot substitute for treating clients well, running a good jobsite, respecting trade partners, or standing behind what you build. Your reputation still has to be earned.

    In a recent development, once you’ve earned it, however, there is nothing wrong with helping it travel. That doesn’t require becoming a marketer. It simply means being a little more intentional about making the work, knowledge, and people behind your firm visible.

    Industry observers note that and there is a benefit beyond finding the kinds of projects you want. The same things that help clients, architects, designers, and trade partners understand your company also help potential employees understand it. Most builder websites show houses, but far fewer show the people behind them. A good carpenter who is considering their next move may want to know what kinds of projects they would work on, who they would work alongside, whether people stay, and whether there is room to grow.

    Make it easier for future employees and clients alike to understand who you are, what you do well, and where you’re headed. Because good work will lead to more good work, but only if people know about it.

    — Carrie Simmons is director of marketing and a business consultant at HELM Construction Solutions. Photo courtesy of HELM Construction Solutions.

    5 Things You Should Take Out of Your Garage Before Winter

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    It has been revealed that while it’s convenient to treat your garage as an all-purpose storage area, plummeting temperatures can ruin valuable gear and create serious safety risks for your family. Before it gets too cold outside, you’ll want to remove certain items from your unheated garage and find a more appropriate storage space. We asked professional organizer Lori Bailey, founder and owner of Miss Organized in the Newly introduced York/New Jersey area, about the most common household goods that are typically stored in a garage but shouldn’t be, and where to keep them instead.

    In a recent development, avoid storing perishable food and canned goods in the garage. This includes rice, beans, soup, dried fruit, nuts, cereal, pasta, canned and bottled drinks, and even pet food. “I will often see people use their garages as an extension of their pantry, especially when they buy in bulk,” indicates Bailey. “However, canned foods should not be exposed to freezing temperatures since that can compromise the seal and safety of the food.” This can result in bacteria entering and spoiling the food.

    It has been revealed that cans also can burst, or the food itself could actually freeze, which can ruin its taste and texture. In addition, food that comes in cardboard packaging is vulnerable to pests like rodents and insects. “Your pantry, kitchen cabinets, or a storage room in the basement are much better options for your food,” advises Bailey.

    In a recent development, paint is one of the most common items that Bailey sees stored in garages, but extreme cold can actually ruin it. “When paint freezes, it can separate and become lumpy, making it unusable.” Some paint can even get ruined before your thermometer drops to 32 degrees Fahrenheit; latex paint, for example, should be stored in a place that doesn’t drop below 50 degrees Fahrenheit. Chemicals such as cleaners, solvents, and automotive fluids also can spoil, leak, or even become a fire hazard if stored in an unheated garage during winter. Bring these products inside and store them in a well-ventilated and temperature-controlled area, such as a basement utility room, laundry room, or storage closet, says Bailey.

    Critical paperwork like passports and birth certificates, photographs, children’s artwork, and sentimental keepsakes should never be stored in an unheated garage, says Bailey. “I always tell my clients that paper clutter needs a proper home since moisture and temperature fluctuations can cause paper to warp, photographs to stick together, and sentimental items to deteriorate.” Rodents can also get in and destroy papers. Bailey recommends keeping these items in labeled, protective containers inside your home.

    With a heat resistance of up to 5,200 degrees Fahrenheit and a lock, this storage bag offers exceptional protection for your valuable documents.

    Sources indicate that leaving sensitive electronics, battery-operated devices, and batteries in an unheated garage over the winter can also be problematic, permanently ruining their internal components and drastically shortening their lifespan. This includes everything from standard household batteries to rechargeable power tool batteries and lawn mower batteries. Temperature swings can cause delicate microchips and circuitry to expand and contract, as well as condensation that can lead to rust and corrosion. To protect your gear and maintain peak performance, relocate all electronic devices and remove batteries from your tools before the first freeze, storing them in a dry, temperature-controlled area of your home.

    Bailey also sees many people storing holiday decorations in their garages. However, some of those items, even if placed in bins, can’t withstand freezing temperatures. “Candles can crack or warp, and certain decorative materials, adhesives, and finishes can deteriorate,” warns Bailey. “I always encourage my clients to be selective about what goes into seasonal storage and to keep temperature-sensitive decorations indoors.”.

    #181762. 23 Cheerful Houseplants That Bloom in Winter

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1988 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Bobvila ↗ Open Full Page

    23 Cheerful Houseplants That Bloom in Winter

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • In a recent development, winter is a long season of brown lawns, bare trees, and frost-covered shrubs.
    • Typically a summer bloomer, jasmine can bloom during the winter, adding sweet fragrance to indoor spaces.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    In a recent development, winter is a long season of brown lawns, bare trees, and frost-covered shrubs. Our feeling is that if we can’t get color and cheer in outdoor beds this time of year, we may as well cultivate some color indoors. Poinsettias are common, colorful blooms for this season, but aren’t for everyone because they’re toxic to pets, according to the ASPCA. But who notes your wintertime plant picks have to be Christmas-themed, or even red? Try these cheerful houseplants on for size, or gift them to your nearest and dearest this season.

    Typically a summer bloomer, jasmine can bloom during the winter, adding sweet fragrance to indoor spaces. To encourage rebloom the following year, give it a time-out in the fall in a room that is completely dark at night. Exposure to street light or indoor lighting will interrupt the cycle. Give this nontoxic plant a trim once it blooms, since jasmine tends to get leggy.

    From December to April, cyclamen, which can bloom for weeks, sends up lightly fragrant flowers above heart-shaped, silver-marbled foliage. After flowering, the plant loses its leaves and dies back for the summer. Some owners might be tempted to toss spent cyclamens into the trash, but take note: The plant is not dead, just dormant. Continue to water it once in a while and when temperatures cool, it will start growing again. Cyclamen is toxic and should be kept away from cats, dogs, and kids.

    Recent findings suggest that these striking succulent houseplants have been popular holiday gifts since the 1800s. Although named for its cactus-like foliage, Christmas cactus needs a little more water than its name suggests. Getting this nontoxic plant to rebloom takes a bit of coaxing in the form of light and temperature control, but it’s so worth it.

    In mid-October, start giving the plant long nights of total darkness, 13 hours or more, in temperatures between 55 and 65 degrees, to trigger flower bud production. When buds appear, put the plant back in a sunny indoor location.

    Industry observers note that despite their odorous reputation, paperwhites are a perfect pick-me-up plant, provided you steer clear of ‘Ziva’, a common (and smelly) variety that can swiftly stink up an entire room. Opt for other paperwhites like ‘Cheerfulness’ and ‘Erlicheer’, which have a less-offensive aroma. Paperwhites don’t require prechilling and are easy to spot in late fall at major-box stores or online from specialty bulb companies. This plant, too, should be kept away from pets and kids, since it is toxic.

    Rosemary probably won’t bloom, but the scent alone is uplifting enough. The plant is easy enough to procure during the holidays and can often be found in playful topiary shapes, including that of a Christmas tree. Place it in a sunny kitchen window where it can do double duty as decoration and culinary herb.

    While rosemary isn’t harmful to pets or people in normal quantities, if your cat takes an outsize liking to the plant, move it out of reach, as it can be irritating in large quantities.

    One of the most interesting succulents around, desert rose grows in a mini tree shape and produces stunning flowers. As you would do for other succulents, water desert rose sparingly. Thick stems give rise to flowers in solid colors—some varieties even have striping—that bloom throughout the year.

    It has been revealed that after flowering, it’s common for the plant to shed its leaves until fresh growth emerges in the summer, so don’t give up on it. This is another one to keep away from pets and kids as it is poisonous, particularly to cats.

    Recent findings suggest that they get a bad rap for being fussy, but growing orchids is actually pretty simple, provided you offer them bright but indirect light and ample humidity. Water orchids thoroughly and allow them to dry out between waterings. Blooms last for months, so it’s best to choose a plant with buds that haven’t yet opened to get as much longevity out of them as possible. These beauties are nontoxic and safe for households with pets and kids.

    Crane’s 4-in-1 Drop Ultrasonic Cool Mist Humidifier is compact, budget-friendly, and humidifies houseplants without making the home feel damp.

    Situate the diminutive, nontoxic African violet plant in bright, indirect light and enjoy months of continuous flowering in shades of red, white, purple, and everything in between. Set yourself up for gardening success by picking up a specialized African violet pot with a slow-release wicking reservoir in the bottom that prevents damage to the leaves from overhead watering.

    Give them bright, indirect light and plenty of humidity and you’ll enjoy a flower frenzy all winter long from indoor begonias. Dry air may be the norm at this time of year, but it’s a death knell for begonias, so set your plant on a shallow tray of water filled with pebbles to humidify the air around it. As much as they like water, too much of a good thing can be harmful. It’s best to water when the plant shows signs of thirst, such as drooping leaves. While begonias are not toxic to humans, they are toxic to pets.

    According to recent reports, A peace lily can add verdant height (up to 6 feet, in fact) to a drab corner of your home this winter. Several white flag-like flowers, which are really spathes, grace this beautiful but unpredictable plant. It can be hard to determine when and if a peace lily will flower, but it tends to send up stems in February, provided it receives sufficient bright, indirect light. Keep this toxic plant away from pets and kids.

    One of the more unusual and upright houseplants, flowering maple blooms almost nonstop. Palmate maple-like leaves and pendulous flowers resembling Chinese lanterns make for a display that will invite plenty of comments. The variegated leaves of certain varieties up the interest, but variegated and non-variegated leaves can be irritating to skin so you might want to wear gloves while working with this plant. Flowering maple is nontoxic to pets.

    Amaryllis bulbs produce spectacular trumpet-shaped flowers. Timing is everything with this plant: Bulbs should be planted approximately 6 weeks before you want flowers. Once the flowering stops, snip the stalk a few inches above the bulb.

    Recent findings suggest that to encourage rebloom, remove the bulb from the soil in September and keep it in a cool, dark environment for 2 months before repotting. Think carefully about where you’ll place amaryllis: It can cause severe gastrointestinal distress to pets and people.

    According to recent reports, like amaryllis and Christmas cactus, clivias need a chilling period to trigger the development of clusters of orange or yellow lily-like flowers. With no need for high humidity, clivia is perfectly suited to indoor life and will survive the winter in a bright, north-facing window. Kaffir lily contains small amounts of the alkaloid lycorine, which is toxic to humans and pets if consumed in large quantities.

    Industry observers note that not to be confused with bleeding heart plant (Dicentra spectabilis), bleeding heart vine is a beautiful climbing plant that produces long-lasting clusters of pink or partly red flowers when placed in a sunny window. Give it a trellis or support to climb, and prune back hard after flowering to keep it under control. Don’t worry about pets and kids getting close; this one’s nontoxic.

    According to recent reports, one of the easiest houseplants to grow and find, kalanchoe tosses out clusters of flowers in deeply saturated hues. The trick is preventing the tropical succulent from becoming too leggy. Pinch it back after flowering and a rebloom should be close behind. Keep this one away from pets and kids, as it is toxic.

    Enjoy large daisy-like flowers indoors with cineraria. Compact clusters of daisy-like flowers sit atop large dark green leaves. Flowers can be red, purple, blue, or white, and each flower has a center eye surrounded by a small white ring. Purchase plants with plenty of buds to get the most out of the bloom period, and keep this poisonous plant away from pets and children.

    What many consider a flower is really a spathe that emerges from the plant in hues of red, pink, white, and variegated colors. Each spathe displays a contrasting white or yellow flower spike within. Anthurium prefers bright light and high humidity, which may be challenging in a heated home. Place the plant on a shallow pebble-and-water-filled tray, away from kids and pets, to increase the humidity.

    Not to be confused with hardy azaleas, greenhouse azaleas are meant to be grown indoors and will not survive if planted in the garden. Select plants with plenty of unopened buds to increase the amount of time you can enjoy its blooms, and be sure not to let the soil dry out. Swallowing large quantities of this plant can spell trouble for pets and humans, so if your dog is a habitual plant snacker, keep azaleas safely away.

    Traditionally grown as a perennial, today’s gloxinias are bred to produce masses of blooms without regard for the long-term health of the plant. By the time they’ve finished flowering, the plant simply has nothing left. For this reason, it’s just as well to think of this nontoxic plant as an annual and treat it well while it’s in bloom: keep it in bright, indirect light, water it enough to keep the soil moist, and feed it with a high-phosphorus liquid plant food every 2 weeks.

    As the name implies, the flowers on this columnea resemble small goldfish in shades of red, orange, or yellow. Trailing dark green foliage makes the goldfish plant an excellent choice for a hanging planter in bright light. As with African violets, avoid getting water on its leaves, which will cause browning and, in some cases, fungal problems. If your cats are tempted by the goldfish plant, as they might be by actual goldfish, worry not: This plant is harmless to pets.

    Add a taste of the tropics to your indoor winterscape with lipstick plant, a vining beauty that looks fantastic in a hanging basket or cascading down a tall piece of furniture. The red, tubular flowers of this nontoxic plant are an exciting and vibrant contrast to its glossy dark green foliage. The plant prefers bright, indirect sunlight and temperatures of 65 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit. It appreciates a bit of humidity, so keep a spray bottle handy, and also apply a slow-release fertilizer once a month.

    The leaves of this brightly hued plant resemble those of a shamrock, though they’re much larger and they’re purple. This South American native also produces delicate five-petaled flowers in white or pink that show off during the day but button up at night. Oxalis likes humidity and temperatures of 65 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit. Keep purple shamrock plants in bright direct light, but out of reach of pets and children, as it is toxic and can be quite irritating and even dangerous if ingested.

    If you can get past this succulent’s thorniness and toxicity, crown of thorns makes an intriguing addition to a houseplant collection. Its thick, thorn-covered stems support clumps of 2- to 6-inch-long medium-green leaves topped by clusters of small pink, white, or yellow flowers that bloom year-round. Put it in a sunny spot and fertilize it monthly. Note that this is a good plant for those who are stingy with the watering can, since it doesn’t mind drying out. It’s not good, however, for households with pets or kids, as it’s prickly and poisonous.

    In a recent development, doing home projects out in a garage or down in a basement workshop isn’t always possible. And even when it is possible, it’s not always the best option, especially if you need to carry heavy, oversized, or delicate materials throughout your home. Instead, it’s sometimes better to set up a temporary workshop where you need to work.

    After years spent as a construction project manager moving my tools and materials between warehouses, work sites, and the homes/businesses of our customers, I developed an easy system for setting up a quick and effective temporary workshop with just a few key components. Keep reading to find out exactly what you need to create your own temporary workshop at your home.

    Working on the floor strains your back, while working on dining tables risks costly dents and scratches. Instead, it’s always good to have a portable workbench that’s easy to set up and take down, like the Keter Folding Workbench. A stable and reliable surface makes projects more efficient, since you won’t need to be bending over to cut, glue, or drill.

    Industry observers note that additionally, the workbench can act as a simple support when you need to measure materials, set up a miter saw, or clamp your materials so that they don’t shift while you work. If you don’t want to purchase or build a new workbench for this purpose, you can also set up a pair of heavy-duty collapsible sawhorses paired with a sacrificial plywood sheet to give you a waist-high surface that folds flat for storage.

    According to recent reports, floor and countertop protection prevents permanent damage and can reduce your cleanup time by half. For this reason, it’s essential to initiative for surface protection and cleanup when you are setting up your temporary workshop.

    In a recent development, drape moving blankets or thick canvas drop cloths over tables, counters, or hardwood floors to absorb impacts and catch dropped tools. Unlike plastic tarps, heavy canvas stays put and prevents items from sliding around. To help keep your temporary workshop clean and organized, include a small wet/dry shop vac fitted with a disposable fleece filter bag to capture messes at the source so you can pack up in minutes.

    Sources indicate that treated with a special coating, this heavy-duty tarp repels moisture in addition to offering protection to your work surface. Learn more.

    Without a heavy, bolted-down bench vise, clamps act as your third hand to hold materials steady while cutting, gluing, or drilling. Keep two or three medium-sized bar clamps handy to secure materials directly to a table edge or sawhorse. These clamps are often easy to store when not in use, so they won’t get in the way while you work.

    Also, you can lay a rubberized mesh pad, like this POWERTEC Nonslip Mat, under smaller pieces when sanding or routing. It holds flat workpieces steady using friction alone, leaving the entire top surface unobstructed.

    In a recent development, overhead room lighting casts shadows right over your hands when you lean over a project to see what you are doing, increasing mistakes and safety risks. But holding a flashlight while you work just ties up one of your hands, severely limiting your control and efficiency. Instead, it’s better to find task lights that are made for versatility so you can focus on the project, rather than fighting with dim lighting.

    A directional light clipped to a shelf, chair, or table edge lets you aim bright light directly at your cut line or assembly area. Opt for a high-lumen LED clamp light or magnetic work light to illuminate your temporary workshop, like this ZONE LED Clamp Work Light.

    It has been revealed that indoor outlets are often far from where you need to work and rarely have enough open receptacles. A 12-gauge, multi-outlet cord with built-in GFCI protection, such as this CCCEI Extension Cord, safely handles high-draw power tools while protecting you from electrical faults. It can also be used to power a space heater for a temporary cold weather workshop upgrade if you need to work outside or in an uninsulated space.

    It has been revealed that use a thick-gauge cord to safely run high-draw power tools from a wall outlet to your temporary station without overheating or losing power. Additionally, use a surge-protected power strip with wide-spaced outlets for your battery chargers, task lights, and smaller tools. Wide spacing prevents bulky power bricks from blocking adjacent plugs.
